## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
check to the same fixture bar.

**When a rule mandates a *form*, the check asserts that form — never the intent behind it.** Where
the prose says *write it exactly like this*, the check's whole job is deciding whether the artifact
is that form; inferring what the author meant is unbounded in the wrong direction and leaves the
likeliest reproduction uncaught, since a hand-picked marker list always misses the phrasing nobody
enumerated. Expect a form check to fire on something that breaks the form while causing no harm —
that's the rule as written doing its job, not a reason to re-add intent-guessing.

When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the
candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.

## Coming out: the deletion test

Coming out of a conversion, apply the **deletion test**: prose a mechanism fully covers is
deleted, never trimmed. Ask it of every paragraph standing beside a landed check — *with this
paragraph gone, would the check still catch every violation it describes **and** tell the agent
how to fix it?* If yes, it is redundant: delete it whole. The check's failure message is where
the rule lives now and its header comment is where the rationale lives, so a paragraph restating
either pays twice and is the drift trap waiting to spring.

Before concluding prose is the only carrier, look at the pack's **skills** too — an
activity-scoped skill often already holds the map a rule is repeating. Keep only what no artifact
carries.

The test **discriminates** rather than just deleting: a paragraph stays whole whenever it carries
something the check does not — a second rule in the same breath, an exemption the check can't
encode, a value the check can't judge, or a remedy the finding's own `fix` line never states
(a finding renders `what` / `why` / `fix` / `doc`, never the rule's `description`, so a remedy
that lives only in the description is not carried). Two worked calls: an `npm test` invariant
went entirely — the check caught it and the testing-guide skill already listed the suites —
while an `extension-test/` mirror bullet stayed, because the check beside it enforced only the
`package.json` list's sync with the tree and never the mirror convention itself.

Whether a check covers a rule is a judgment about meaning, so this test is applied by a
**reader**, not mechanized.

## Bounds

- **One PR, bounded surface** — the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture, and the
  trimmed prose. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there.
- **Never delete a rule you didn't convert** — the deletion test is only ever asked of a rule a
  *landed* check now enforces.
- Run the suite and the sweep green before the PR goes up, and never push to `main` directly. The
  sweep opens its own PR for the owner's approval; the upgrade pass adds its conversion to the
  growth-extract PR already being opened, and opens none of its own.

---

# Working in the canary

This repo is Claudinite's **live canary**. Read this before changing anything here, because the
normal instinct — make the repo green, make the repo useful — is wrong in a specific way.

## The gate this repo is half of

Canon CI can prove a canon change is internally consistent. It cannot prove the change is safe for
**consumers**: the vendored mount, the pack loader, the hook wiring and the skill mounts only meet
a real repo on the other side of a vendor set. So the canon runs
`.github/workflows/canary-rehearsal.yml`, which converges *this* repo against a candidate canon ref
and runs the world sweep and the selftest against the result.

The gate's whole value rests on this repo being a **real, disposable member**. Real, or the
rehearsal tests a shape no consumer has. Disposable, or nobody will let the rehearsal converge it.

## What must not be removed

Anything that makes this a member is load-bearing:

- the vendored mount at `.claudinite/shared/` and the `.claudinite-checks.json` declaration
  that names what is vendored;
- the `.claude/settings.json` hook registrations;
- the vendored scheduler workflow, with the repo-hashed cron minute;
- the unfiltered conformance workflow;
- **the `local/canary` pack** — the highest-value shape here. Canon #555 broke the fleet through
  exactly this surface: a local pack's manifest, its rules in both scopes, its bundled skills.

## Reading a red rehearsal

A rehearsal failure is a claim about the **candidate canon ref**, not about this repo. Before
touching anything here, separate the two:

1. **Does the same failure reproduce against canon `main`?** If it does, the canary drifted or
   broke on its own and the candidate ref is exonerated. Re-baseline to `main` and re-run.
2. **Only the candidate ref fails?** That is the signal the gate exists to produce. Fix it in the
   canon. Do not fix it here — a canary patched to stay green is a canary that has stopped
   reporting.
3. **Never quiet a finding with an `accept` entry to get a rehearsal green.** An `accept` is a
   reasoned keep about *this repo's* content; using one to mask a canon regression converts a
   loud failure into a silent one, permanently.

## Repairing the canary

Re-baselining to canon `main` is always the correct repair, and there is no local state here worth
preserving. One caveat, from vendoring's anti-rewind guard (#328): the stamped `ref` in
`.claudinite-checks.json` must be an **ancestor of canon `main`**. Stamp a feature-branch sha and
the repo lands `ref-not-on-trunk`, which convergence then refuses to rewind past — wedging the
repo permanently. Rehearsals may stamp a candidate ref by design; a human repair should not.

1	// WHERE A MEMBER'S SETTINGS LIVE — the one place the declaration's filename is
2	// spelled, for every reader in the corpus: the checks loader, the update and
3	// install flows, the vendor writer, the migration ops, and the cross-repo
4	// readers that fetch the file over the API rather than off disk.
5	//
6	// THE RENAME (#1252). The file is `.claudinite-settings.json`. It was
7	// `.claudinite-checks.json` when checks were the only thing a member declared,
8	// and it has not been a file of checks for a long time: it carries the pack
9	// declaration, the scheduler anchor, the installed versions and the delivery
10	// override. The old name is still READ, everywhere, because a member's file is
11	// renamed by a migration record that converges on its own schedule — and until
12	// every member has run it, both names name the same file.
13	//
14	// The tolerance is the LEGACY half of a rename with a stated end: the cleanup
15	// that deletes it is gated on no member still carrying the old name, never on a
16	// date (#1252 Phase 3). Read order is new-then-legacy, so a member mid-rename
17	// that somehow holds both is read from the one the migration wrote.
18	import { existsSync } from 'node:fs';
19	import { join } from 'node:path';
20	
21	export const SETTINGS_FILE = '.claudinite-settings.json';
22	
23	// Retired from what anything WRITES; still read while members carry it.
24	export const LEGACY_SETTINGS_FILE = '.claudinite-checks.json';
25	
26	// Both names, newest first — the read order. Exported for the cross-repo readers,
27	// which have no disk to probe and must try the paths in this order over the API.
28	export const SETTINGS_FILES = [SETTINGS_FILE, LEGACY_SETTINGS_FILE];
29	
30	// The settings file to READ under `root`: whichever name is actually there, the
31	// new one when both are, and the new one when neither is — so a caller reporting
32	// "no settings file" names the file a member should now have rather than the one
33	// being retired.
34	export function settingsPath(root) {
35	  for (const name of SETTINGS_FILES) {
36	    const path = join(root, name);
37	    if (existsSync(path)) return path;
38	  }
39	  return join(root, SETTINGS_FILE);
40	}
41	
42	// Is this path one of the two settings-file names? For the scans that ask whether
43	// a changed file is the declaration, which must keep answering yes for a member
44	// that has not been renamed yet.
45	export const isSettingsFile = (path) => SETTINGS_FILES.includes(String(path ?? '').split('/').pop());

# Claudinite work-item executor (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §6, §10) — a pull worker
# over the queue. ONE RUN DRAINS THE QUEUE (§15.30, reversing §15.22's one-item
# run): Actions bills each job's minutes rounded up, so a run per item paid a
# whole invocation — checkout, setup, rounding — for each one. A run now settles
# its items one at a time until nothing is pickable, and the continuation job
# below covers a run that dies mid-drain. It carries NO cron of its own — the
# scheduler run's hourly dispatch, made when that run leaves something pickable,
# is the guaranteed delivery, so a lost `task:ready` label event is latency lost
# and never work lost.
#
# THIS IS THE ONLY PLACE SECRETS LIVE (DESIGN §14). The wiring converge stamps
# every task's declared `required_secrets`, plus each configured invocation
# endpoint's token secret, into the step env below by name — the scheduler run and the
# janitor get none, because they never execute task code. Code-work is the only task
# code that ever sees a value; the agent hop carries nothing.
#
# MORE CAPACITY IS MORE EXECUTORS. Nothing enumerates them and each claim is
# independently leased, so a second job, a matrix width, or a runner outside
# Actions entirely all work — the executor's whole interface is issue read/write
# plus the repo at HEAD.
name: Claudinite executor

on:
  issues:
    types: [labeled]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      continuation_depth:
        description: 'How many dead runs this chain has continued through — set by the continuation job below, never by hand'
        required: false
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

jobs:
  execute:
    # A label event on anything else is not this workflow's business — and a
    # workflow_dispatch carries no label at all, so it always runs.
    # BOTH READY SPELLINGS, for as long as any fielded engine writes the legacy one
    # (#1119). A workflow's event trigger names label strings LITERALLY — nothing
    # here decodes — so this list is the one place the migration's two vocabularies
    # must both appear, and dropping the legacy spelling early makes every item an
    # older engine readies wait for the hourly scheduler run instead of starting now.
    if: >-
      github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:status:waiting-for-executor'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:ready'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:urgent'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # The old cap — ≤ the engine's executing leash — retired with the heartbeat
    # (§15.15). A run is bounded by a DRAIN's work now, and a holder that is alive
    # says so on its item every 15 minutes, so the leash reclaims silence rather
    # than length. What is left here is a backstop against a wedged runner, well
    # clear of any declared `code_work_timeout`; a drain the platform kills at it
    # hands its remainder to the continuation job like any other dead run.
    timeout-minutes: 350
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Pick up and execute ready work
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          # The operator hold (DESIGN §8): set this repo variable to `true` and
          # every entry point exits at its first act, having fired nothing.
          CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL: ${{ vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL }}
          # The wiring converge stamps every declared required_secret, and every
          # configured invocation endpoint's token, below this marker — by name.
          # claudinite:secrets
          CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
          FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs

  # A run that dies — crash, timeout, cancellation, runner loss — never reaches
  # its own re-dispatch, so without this the queue would sit until the next cron
  # fire. The platform runs this job on a FRESH runner after any such death
  # (DESIGN §10, S36), and its one step fires that dispatch instead: the
  # remainder drains in ~a minute, while the dead run's OWN item waits for the
  # executing leash to reclaim it — nothing here touches that item.
  #
  # `continuation_depth` is the stop. A run that dies at startup — a broken
  # engine, a revoked token — dies identically every time, and an unguarded
  # continuation would dispatch itself for as long as that lasts. After three the
  # chain stops and SAYS SO on the repo's workflow-failure issue: a queue that has
  # quietly stopped draining is the one failure nothing else here would surface,
  # since every individual run looks like an ordinary death.
  continue-the-chain:
    needs: execute
    if: failure() || cancelled()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      actions: write
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const depth = Number('${{ inputs.continuation_depth }}' || 0) + 1;
            const ref = context.payload.repository?.default_branch
              ?? context.ref.replace('refs/heads/', '');
            const run = `${context.serverUrl}/${context.repo.owner}/${context.repo.repo}/actions/runs/${context.runId}`;
            if (depth <= 3) {
              await github.rest.actions.createWorkflowDispatch({
                owner: context.repo.owner,
                repo: context.repo.repo,
                workflow_id: 'claudinite-executor.yml',
                ref,
                inputs: { continuation_depth: String(depth) },
              });
              core.info(`the executor run died — dispatched a fresh one on ${ref} (continuation ${depth} of 3)`);
              return;
            }
            // The chain has died three times running: this is not one bad runner,
            // and dispatching a fourth would spend the day proving it. Escalate to
            // the same one-open-issue surface the scheduler's own failures use, and
            // let the hourly scheduler run be what tries again.
            const { owner, repo } = context.repo;
            const title = 'Claudinite executor chain failed repeatedly';
            // The platform reporting its own failure IS an origin (`task:origin:github`),
            // and a chain that has died three times is a break to diagnose — the
            // `failure` park, the one lane that holds a task's lane (#1119).
            const labels = ['workflow-failure', 'task:origin:github', 'task:status:needs-human-failure'];
            const ensure = [
              { name: 'workflow-failure', color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite scheduler: a scheduler run or task failed' },
              { name: 'task:origin:github', color: 'd4c5f9', description: 'Claudinite queue: filed by the platform itself — a workflow reporting its own failure' },
              { name: 'task:status:needs-human-failure', color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite queue: parked — the run broke, diagnose and fix' },
            ];
            for (const l of ensure) await github.rest.issues.createLabel({ owner, repo, ...l }).catch(() => {});
            const body = `Three consecutive executor runs died before finishing their item. The chain stops here; the next hourly scheduler run will dispatch a fresh one.\n\nThe last run: ${run}`;
            const found = await github.rest.search.issuesAndPullRequests({ q: `repo:${owner}/${repo} is:issue is:open in:title "${title}"` });
            if (found.data.total_count > 0) await github.rest.issues.createComment({ owner, repo, issue_number: found.data.items[0].number, body });
            else await github.rest.issues.create({ owner, repo, title, labels, body });
            core.setFailed('the executor chain died three times in a row — escalated');
